title: Assessing Scene Generation Techniques for Testing COLREGS-Compliance of Autonomous Surface Vehicles
abstract: Autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) need to complete missions without posing risks to other maritime traffic. Safe traffic in open sea encounters is controlled by the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) formulated by the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Designed with human operators in mind, the COLREGS are intentionally underspecified, which may result in ambiguous requirements for correct behaviour for ASVs. Hence the systematic testing of such ambiguous situations is particularly important. This paper investigates to what extent existing test scenario generation approaches deemed effective in the automotive domain can be adapted to test COLREGS-compliance in a maritime context with multi-vessel encounters. In a series of experiments involving synthetic and real-world test scenarios, their performance is evaluated with respect to relevance, diversity, completeness, scalability and speed. Our results indicate that (1) test scenarios derived from historic maritime traffic are insufficient for testing multi-ship encounters. Moreover, (2) existing test scenario generation techniques provide sufficient scalability and speed, but they are very limited in terms of diversity and completeness when the number of vessels increases.
venue: ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2025)
introduction:
In recent years, significant efforts have been made to develop autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) for civilian and military purposes. A key challenge in developing ASVs is to ensure that they can navigate safely without endangering other vessels. Specifically, any vessel operating in international waters must comply with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) [19], a set of rules standardized by the International Maritime Organization. COL-REGS regulate how a vessel (referred to as own ship, or OS) should navigate to avoid a potential collision when it encounters another vessel (the target ship, or TS) on a near-intercept course.

Significant effort has been put into developing COLREGS compliant control software (see, for example, [73]), and maritime simulators [2,72] for full-stack testing of ASVs in virtual environments. However, there is currently a lack of effective means for systematic validation of COLREGS compliance. Existing work either relies on manually designed test scenarios [10,47,53,68,79] or scenarios extracted from historical traffic data [5,40,43,46,76,85]. Unfortunately, none of these approaches offer a proper solution for the safety assurance of ASVs, as the former does not scale to scenarios with a large number of vessels, and the latter is unlikely to cover rare critical scenarios.

Although there is a significant body of work on synthesizing high-quality test scenarios for autonomous road vehicles [1,3,6,8,13,27,34,54,75], the maritime domain is highly different, hence these techniques are not directly applicable for testing COLREGS compliance. Particular challenges posed by the maritime domain compared to the automotive domain include:

• Completely different vessel dynamics. Compared to road vehicles, the physical interactions between actors and the environment are more complex in the maritime domain, where vessel dynamics are influenced by the shape of the hull, and external forces such as waves, currents and wind. Moreover, the visibility range is of significant maritime concern, as distances between actors are several orders of magnitude greater than between road vehicles. • Less constrained geometry. The spatial relations of actors in the automotive domain are restricted by road geometry, which is in turn restricted to adhere to a finite set of road design elements (intersections, roundabouts, lanes, etc.) and traffic rules. This makes the search space of possible physical actor relations comparably much smaller than in the maritime domain, where actors can have any relative position, heading, and speed. The higher degrees of freedom makes, among other things, stochastic testing (which is widely used in the automotive domain [36,82]) largely infeasible for testing COLREGS compliance. • More diverse classes of actors. The size difference of actors (hence, their manoeuvring capabilities) is at most 2-3 orders of magnitude for road vehicles (e.g., motorcycle vs. semi-truck), while it can be up to 6 orders of magnitude in maritime (e.g., small motor boat vs. oil tanker). • Free-form trajectories. An implication of the two points above is that maritime vessel trajectories are constrained not by a predetermined road geometry, but rather by the COLREGS rules, by the manoeuvrability of the vessel, and by external dynamics (currents, wind, etc.). Therefore, generating a test scenario for the maritime domain involves two principal steps:

(1) generation of an initial scene, which defines initial actor placements, headings, and speeds; and (2) generation of vessel trajectories evolving from the initial scene. • Underspecified traffic rules. Being designed with human operators in mind, the COLREGS are deliberately underspecified, leaving significant room for individual judgement by ship crew when making decisions. As a consequence, the COLREGS can become ambiguous for multiship encounters, i.e., COLREGS compliant behaviour w.r.t. one vessel can lead to a rule violation (and risk of collision) w.r.t. another vessel.

Based on this, and further interactions with maritime experts in an ongoing project, we can formulate the following desiderata for an ideal maritime test scenario generator: D1 Relevance. Each test case should represent a hazardous situation that may lead to a potential collision (or other safety violations) if the OS fails to take appropriate action. While relevance is difficult to quantify, according to [41], ambiguous COLREGS situations represent a particularly relevant subclass of test scenarios as identified by maritime experts. D2 Diversity. An ideal scenario generator should produce semantically different test cases to avoid the redundant testing of equivalent COLREGS scenarios. This is especially important if test scenarios are executed in computationally expensive, high-fidelity simulators. D3 Completeness. Related to the notion of diversity, an ideal scenario generator should enumerate all semantically distinct COLREGS scenarios for a given number of vessels. In particular, for safety assurance, it is important to cover not only common types of encounters, but also rare safety-critical edge cases (e.g. ambiguous COLREGS situations). D4 Scalability. To cover more complex scenarios, such as those exhibiting ambiguity, the scenario generator must be capable of scaling to a larger number of vessels. D5 Speed. Since a large number of scenarios might be needed to cover the space of possible COLREGS situations, the time for generating a single scenario is also an important factor.

In this experience report, we investigate existing state-of-the-art scenario generation approaches from the automotive domain, and evaluate to what degree they are applicable to the maritime domain with regards to D1-D5 above. In particular,

• We formalize the (informally presented) COLREGS model proposed in [41], and extend it to handle an arbitrary number of actors (i.e., vessels) for open sea encounters. • We formally define logical scenarios and initial scenes for open sea encounters in the maritime domain with their geometric constraints (analogously to logical scenes in multi-level abstractions for scene concretization in the automotive domain [3]). • We adapt two scenario generation approaches widely used in the automotive domain (searchbased scenario generation (SB) [1,6,8,34], and rejection-sampling, used by the state-of-the-art Scenic tool (RS) [27,75,81]) to generate initial scenes in the the maritime domain. • In a series of experiments involving the automated generation of initial scenes, we evaluate the two approaches with respect to D1-D5. We also compare the synthesized scenes with CommonOcean (CO) [43], a recently published dataset of historical maritime traffic collected using public AIS (automatic identification system) data.

In this paper, we exclusively focus on the generation of initial scenes, which is the conceptually hard problem in scenario generation for the maritime domain. Subsequently, concrete trajectories of vessels can be generated from the initial scenes by various approaches [24,57,70]. The scope of our investigations is limited to open sea encounters involving multiple vessels.

Up to our best knowledge, our paper provides the first cross-domain adaptation of test scenario generation techniques developed for automotive in the maritime domain. Moreover, it provides a systematic evaluation of various key quality attributes (derived with the involvement of maritime experts) on both synthetic and real-world test scenarios. Moreover, testing COLREGS-compliance in multi-vessel open sea encounters is another innovative aspect of our work.
experiment:
We conducted experiments to address the following research questions in open sea encounters: • RQ1: How relevant are synthetic and real-world test scenarios for COLREGS-compliance? • RQ2: How diverse and complete are the test scenes generated by synthetic approaches? • RQ3: How scalable and fast are synthetic scene generation approaches?

We refer to the number of vessels in a scenario as the problem size (𝐾), where 𝐾 = |S 𝑁 |. The input parameters for 𝑁 𝐺 ∈ N are detailed in Table 5, reflecting characteristics of small to large-sized ships. For simplicity, length and speed limits are the same across all TSs. We run the scene generation 1000 times with both SB and RS for each problem size with a timeout of 10 minutes. Finally, we abstract each valid concrete scene using l2f for each batch (i.e. particular approach and problem size) into one of the equivalence classes on the functional level, as described in Section 4.3.

Our measurements are conducted on an Ubuntu 24.04 machine with an Intel Core Processor (Haswell, model: 60, family: 6) and 32 GB of RAM using Python 3.12. The pseudo-random seed is reset to ensure reproducibility, the garbage collector is explicitly called, and two warm-up runs are performed before each measurement to initialize the Python cache, enhancing stability.

Motivation. To investigate relevance (D1), RQ1 aims to determine to what extent automatically generated (synthetic) and AIS-based (real-world) test scenarios are relevant, i.e., that they represent hazardous COLREGS scenarios to test the COLREGS-compliance of an OS.

Metrics. Unfortunately, no generally accepted metrics exist which would measure the relevance of a test suite for assessing COLREGS-compliance. However, a minimum requirement for relevance is that the ships in a test scenario are actually in a COLREGS-scenario (see Section 2.2). Furthermore, ambiguous scenarios are known to be relevant for system-level testing in the maritime domain [41]. Hence, for each compared approach, we calculate the ratio of relevant and consistent scenarios (T ∩ C) with respect to the total number of generated scenes. Moreover, we calculate a similar ratio for ambiguous and consistent scenes (A ∩ C).

Compared approaches. We compare two synthetic scenario generation methods with test scenarios obtained from a real-world dataset.

• The search-based approach SB (introduced in Section 5.1) solves the optimization problem l2o 𝑁 𝐺 , where 𝑁 𝐺 ∈ N , using input parameters from Table 5. • The rejection sampling-based approach RS (introduced in Section 5.2) uses a sampling-based strategy for the same problem. • The open-source CommonOcean benchmark [43] CO represents real-world encounter scenarios derived from AIS data collected from various U.S. coastal regions. This benchmark predominantly (97.7%) features two-vessel encounters.

Our techniques SB and RS are expected to provide fully relevant and consistent scenes faithfully representing COLREGS-scenarios. However, there is no such guarantee for the CO benchmark.

Result analysis. Table 6 shows the total number of generated / observed functional scenarios (in the compared datasets), as well as the percentage of relevant+consistent (T ∩ C), and ambigu-ous+consistent (A ∩ C) cases with increasing problem size. Since ambiguity is defined only for multi-vessel scenarios, no ambiguous scenarios exist for 2 vessels.

The real-world CO dataset has low relevance ratio (30.8%) for 𝐾=2 and 0% relevance and ambiguous ratio for 𝐾>2. The low relevance of the dataset prevents its practical use in testing COLREGScompliance for multi-vessel encounters, thus CO is excluded from further investigations below.

In synthetic test suites, a surprising finding is that not all test scenarios are relevant and consistent. After manually investigating some of these outliers, we recognized COLREGS-scenarios which are not supposed to exist according to the assumptions on the possible COLREGS-situations. For example, double crossing (when two vessels are mutually crossing from the left) is ruled out by the COLREGS, but it can be judged in case of certain large velocity differences between two vessels.

Technically, RS presents slightly more relevant and ambiguous test cases for 𝐾 <= 4 than SB, but it does not provide models for 𝐾 > 4. In general, the ratio of relevant cases decreases, while the ratio of ambiguous cases (within the relevant cases) increases as the problem size increases.

RQ1: Synthetic approaches SB and RS generate relevant scenes for testing COLREGS compliance (with relevance ratios 68.1% to 94.6%). While they also generate ambiguous multi-vessel scenarios, but to a lesser extent (39% to 80%). The real-world CO dataset has minimal relevance for multi-ship encounters (0% for 𝐾 ≥ 3), showing the difficulties of using real AIS data as test scenarios.

Approaches?

Motivation. Assessing ASV behaviour in semantically diverse scenarios is key for safety assurance (diversity, D2). Moreover, all relevant and consistent equivalence classes should be covered (completeness, D3) ideally with similar amount of tests to avoid bias. Thus, RQ2 explores to what extent the test suites derived by the synthetic approaches cover semantically different scenarios and how the distribution of samples deviates from the even distribution. We measure the coverage for the total number of equivalence classes derived as graph shapes from the functional models.

Compared approaches. We compare the two synthetic scene generation approaches SB and RS.

Metrics. We use external shape-based model diversity, as introduced by [66], along with neighbourhood shapes from Section 3 to distinguish equivalence classes. Our diversity metric is defined as the coverage of relevant and consistent equivalence classes in T ∩ C by the generated scenes, as well as the coverage for ambiguous and consistent equivalence classes in A ∩ C:

Result analysis. In Table 7, we present a summary of the total number of relevant and consistent classes (|𝐸𝑄 (T ∩ C)|), and ambiguous and consistent classes (|𝐸𝑄 (A ∩ C)|). Moreover, we present the respective equivalence class coverages (Coverage in T ∩ C, and Coverage in A ∩ C).

In Figure 5, each plot illustrates the distribution of equivalence classes within a batch. The x-axis represents the number of samples, while each histogram bar corresponds to an equivalence class. Missing bars indicate that the batch does not cover the respective class.

Both SB and RS achieve 100% coverage in 2-vessel scenarios. As the number of vessels increases, coverage drops differently for each approach. SB shows a nearly linear decline, covering 93.3%, 74.3%, 68.6%, and 49.2% of equivalence classes for 3 to 6 vessels, respectively. In contrast, RS declines rapidly, reaching 0% coverage for 5-and 6-vessel scenarios.

Although SB is generally more diverse than RS, the generation is biased towards certain equivalence classes, and the distribution becomes more skewed as the problem size increases. When comparing the distributions using the Chi-Square Test [30,58], all the p-values indicate sufficient statistical significance (𝑝 < 0.05). However, according to Kullback-Leibler Divergence [45], for the 2-vessel problem, the distributions of SB and RS have low divergence, indicating that they are similarly diverse for small problems.

The results indicate that neither of the scene generation approaches can provide sufficient diversity and completeness over the relevant and consistent equivalence classes. RQ2: SB achieves higher coverage than RS but coverage decreases with the increasing number of vessels. The decline in coverage and completeness highlights the difficulties of ensuring diverse test case generation as complexity grows.

Motivation. Comprehensive testing of ASV behaviour in multi-vessel encounters requires generating a large number of test scenarios for an increasing number of vessels (scalability, D4) within a limited amount of time (speed, D5). Since, neither genetic algorithms (used by SB) nor rejection sampling (used by RS) guarantee that a solution is found, we also assess whether success rates of test generation are adequate for practical use.

Compared approaches. We compare the two synthetic test generation approaches SB and RS.

Metrics. We evaluate the runtime and success rate for SB and RS based on scene generation for an increasing numbers of vessels (problem sizes). In particular, we define:

• Runtime as the time taken to generate a scenario averaged over successful runs. • Success rate as the proportion of runs that produce a valid scenario within a 10-minute timeout. A scene generation is deemed unsuccessful if no solution is found within this limit. • Average time/scene = average runtime success rate , estimating the time to successfully synthesize one scene. Result analysis. Table 8 shows the success rate, as well as the median and average runtime compared to the average time for successful scene generation with the SB and RS approaches across increasing problem sizes.

SB achieves a 100% success rate for all measurements, demonstrating its robustness regardless of problem complexity. In contrast, Scenic performs well for smaller cases but its success rate declines as 𝐾 increases. While it achieves a 100% success rate for 𝐾 = 2 and 𝐾 = 3, its success rate drops significantly to 9.4% for 𝐾 = 4, and it fails completely (0% success) for 𝐾 > 4.

The median and average runtime of SB increases rapidly with the problem size, but it is still manageable with an average of 22.6 seconds for the 6-vessel scenarios. While RS outperforms SB for 𝐾 = 2, its performance drops drastically, converging to the 10-minute limit for 𝐾 = 4.

After running statistical analysis on the runtimes, we conclude that the results are statistically significant based on the Mann-Whitney U-test [48] (𝑝 < 0.05) with high effect size based on Cohen's D [17,30] (|𝑒 | > 0.8). This excludes the 𝐾 = 2 case where (𝑝 = 0.072) and the effect size is small (𝑒 = 0.2), indicating no evidence that the performance of SB and RS differs.

The results imply that SB is generally faster and more robust for large problems, while RS fails to solve logical scenarios when the constraints contain circular dependencies and involve more than 3 actors. These results are aligned with the observations in the automotive domain in [3].

RQ3: SB is robust in terms of success rate (100%), and its runtime is acceptable even with an increasing number of actors for open sea encounters. In contrast, RS struggles with solving more complex problems (𝐾 > 3) and it is generally slower than SB.

Internal validity. This work aims to compare the direct adaptations of two scenario generation approaches popular in the automotive domain to evaluate their effectiveness in the maritime domain. We have striven to adapt the Scenic approach RS as closely as possible to the maritime domain. When implementing SB, we applied various best practices, such as choosing a widely used algorithm and library for search-based test generation (NSGA-II), using hyperparameter tuning, and applying proven design decisions from existing state-of-the-art work. Nevertheless, we cannot fully guarantee that we provide the best possible implementation, hence it is a potential threat to validity. Furthermore, the success rate of RS would likely increase with an increased timeout.

External validity. Due to the informal nature of the COLREGS, it is not possible to formulate a canonical model of COLREGS-compliant behaviour, which constitutes a threat to external validity (i.e., a different formalization of COLREGS may yield different empirical findings). In particular, we do not consider the special COLREGS regulations for vessels with limited manoeuvrability, such as sailing vessels (Rule 18), which is left to future work. Moreover, we exclude dynamic properties from our models, such as the emergence or disappearance of new COLREGS relations due to evasive actions taken by actors. To handle such cases, our models need to incorporate temporal behaviour in the future. In terms of logical model constraints, we use meaningful domain-specific parameters aligned with standards [19,77], but have chosen a simpler circular safety domain [35,39,42,84] in favour of one of the more advanced elliptical domains proposed in the literature [15,18,60,69,77].

Despite potential limitations of our COLREGS model, we believe that it accurately captures the two most important differences between the automotive and maritime domains, namely, the unconstrained scenario geometry, and the underspecified nature of Rules 12-18.

We investigate test scenarios derived from historical AIS data in the context of the CO benchmark, and obtain negative results. While findings might be different in the context of other AIS data, it is highly unlikely that higher relevance would be observed when testing multi-vessel encounters since such encounters are rare in real life, though they present particularly challenging cornercases. Moreover, deriving actual test scenarios from real-world AIS data is a complex challenge.

After the evaluation, we aim to summarize the practical takeaways of our investigations related to the various quality requirements set up for scenario generators in a maritime context. Scenarios derived from real-world AIS data are insufficient for testing multi-ship encounters. The lack of a canonical formalization of COLREGS discussed in Section 7 poses a challenge also when extracting test scenarios from historical traffic data. Varying notions of what constitutes a relevant scenario are used across different studies [42,76,85], which complicates a meaningful comparison of datasets. As a practical example of this problem, the authors of the CO dataset state in [43] that scenarios were selected on the basis of demonstrating "close encounters" between vessels. However, our study finds that the majority of scenarios in CO do not actually meet our definition of relevant scenarios, as the vessels involved were not in situations regulated by COLREGS (e.g., they were not on potential collision courses). Furthermore, multi-ship encounters occur very rarely in test scenarios derived from AIS data [43,76,85]. Thus, such encounters represent rare, but potentially safety-critical edge cases which are unlikely to be sufficiently tested by scenarios derived from existing traffic. All of this clearly highlights the need for systematic synthetic scenario generators for the maritime domain, where the relevance of test cases can be ensured by construction.

Adapting automotive scenario generators may provide sufficient scalability and speed in maritime. As a positive finding of our paper, adapting existing scenario generation techniques that proved to be effective in the automotive domain is technically feasible both for search-based and rejection sampling based approaches. Moreover, search-based scenario generation provided sufficient scalability and speed for deriving test scenarios for open sea encounters with increasing number of vessels for problems of practical size (3-6 vessels). On the other hand, while rejection sampling was proven highly beneficial in the automotive domain, it was not effective in generating maritime test scenarios, most probably, due to the higher degrees of freedom in vessel placement.

Adapting existing techniques lacks diversity and completeness in a maritime setting. As a negative finding and major limitation of existing approaches, both SB and RS failed to cover many equivalence classes, particularly for larger problems with more vessels. This highlights significant quality issues in directly adapting scenario generation techniques from automotive to maritime domains. Moreover, it clearly shows that further research is necessitated to provide mechanisms that enforce diversity and ensure completeness (on a functional level) during test scenario generation.

Potential gaps in COLREGS-assumptions. As a highly unexpected finding (reported in Table 6) synthetic test generation techniques repeatedly derived scenarios where the functional scenario model was inconsistent. This is particularly surprising due to the following reasons:

• By construction, we ensure that the initial scenes derived by the algorithms presented in Section 5 enforce COLREGS-situations between the own ship and the target ships (hence we ensure relevance of the test cases). • The consistency constraints of our functional scenario models (Table 2) were validated manually by maritime experts and automatically by graph generation techniques, hence we had strong confidence in that they faithfully represent the key assumptions and restrictions of COLREGS on a high level of abstraction. • Assuming that the algorithms are correct and our formalization is faithful, then the detected discrepancies may indicate potentially invalid assumptions in some COLREGS-situations. After further investigations, we have found several cases, which are ruled out by the COLREGS (e.g. double crossing from port, when two vessels would be considered to be mutually crossing from the left). Nevertheless, there may be very rare situations when they can be potentially observed, e.g. when there is a large (but not unrealistic) difference between the velocity of two vessels. Investigating the actual existence of such cases in a practical setting is subject to future work.
task_title: Automated Test Scenario Generation for Multi-Vessel COLREGS Compliance in Autonomous Surface Vehicles
background: Autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) must obey the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) to operate safely, but these rules are intentionally underspecified and become ambiguous in multi-vessel encounters. Current testing relies on manually designed scenarios or historical AIS data, which do not scale to complex multi-ship situations or cover rare ambiguous cases. The maritime domain differs fundamentally from road traffic: vessel dynamics are more complex, geometry is unconstrained, actor sizes vary by orders of magnitude, and trajectories are shaped by rules rather than roads, making automotive test generation techniques unsuitable. An ideal test scenario generator must satisfy five key properties: relevance (hazardous, ambiguous situations), diversity (semantically distinct tests), completeness (full coverage of possible encounters), scalability to many vessels, and speed. Existing synthetic generation approaches adapted from automotive testing struggle to provide sufficient diversity and completeness as the number of vessels grows, while real-world AIS data lacks relevance for multi-vessel scenarios. This motivates the need for new techniques that can systematically produce test suites meeting all five desiderata.
research_question: How can a synthetic test scenario generator automatically create multi-vessel COLREGS encounter scenarios that are simultaneously relevant, diverse, complete, scalable, and fast, enabling systematic safety assurance of autonomous surface vessels?

datasets.name: CommonOcean benchmark
datasets.source: GitHub (refer to the CommonOcean project for AIS-based encounter data)
datasets.description: Real-world maritime encounter scenarios extracted from Automatic Identification System (AIS) data, predominantly featuring two-vessel interactions.

datasets.name: COLREGS functional equivalence classes
datasets.description: The exhaustive set of semantically distinct, logically consistent multi-vessel encounter scenarios derived from a formal model of COLREGS rules (based on functional abstraction and graph-shape equivalence). Can be constructed programmatically for a given number of vessels and parameter ranges.

baselines.name: Search-based maritime scenario generation
baselines.reference: Generic adaptation of automotive search-based scene generation: an optimization method that searches initial vessel placements to maximize a COLREGS relevance score.

baselines.name: Rejection-sampling maritime scenario generation
baselines.reference: Generic adaptation of automotive sampling-based scene generation: random drawing of vessel states filtered by COLREGS encounter criteria.

baselines.name: CommonOcean real-world AIS scenarios
baselines.reference: Pre-collected encounter scenarios from the CommonOcean benchmark.

metrics.name: Relevance ratio (T ∩ C)
metrics.definition: Fraction of generated scenarios that are both relevant (vessels are on a COLREGS-defined collision course) and consistent (logically admissible under the formal COLREGS model).

metrics.name: Ambiguous relevance ratio (A ∩ C)
metrics.definition: Among consistent scenarios, the fraction that are ambiguous (more than one interpretation of COLREGS duties exists for at least one vessel).

metrics.name: Equivalence class coverage
metrics.definition: Percentage of all distinct relevant and consistent functional equivalence classes (grouped by abstract encounter shape) that are represented by at least one generated scenario.

metrics.name: Distribution divergence
metrics.definition: A statistical measure (e.g., Kullback-Leibler divergence) quantifying how the empirical distribution of generated scenarios across equivalence classes deviates from a uniform distribution.

metrics.name: Average generation time
metrics.definition: Mean wall-clock time required to produce one valid scenario, averaged over multiple runs for a fixed problem size.

rqs: RQ1: How relevant are the generated test scenarios compared to those produced by search-based, rejection-sampling, and AIS-derived baselines?
RQ2: How diverse and complete is the test suite in terms of covering all semantically distinct relevant encounter classes, and how uniform is the coverage distribution?
RQ3: How does generation time scale with the number of vessels, and how does it compare to existing synthetic approaches?
experiment_setup.target_subject: Autonomous surface vessel collision-avoidance control software required to comply with COLREGS. The system under test is the 'own-ship' controller; scenarios provide initial positions, headings, and speeds of the own-ship and target vessels. Example controllers include open-source marine autopilots (e.g., ArduPilot/Rover, MOOS-IvP) or academic COLREGS-compliance algorithms.
experiment_setup.constraints: Scenario generation must operate at the functional (logical) level without requiring high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulation. Generated scenarios must be processable by a COLREGS rule checker based on the formal model that defines relevance, consistency, and ambiguity. The generator must not rely on pre-existing multi-vessel AIS data. Scalability should be demonstrated up to at least 6 vessels. The evaluation uses the same functional abstraction and vessel parameter ranges as in the reference formal model.

feasibility_notes: The CommonOcean AIS dataset is publicly available. The COLREGS formal model and associated equivalence classes can be implemented from published international regulations and the cited abstraction rules. The baselines (search-based optimization and rejection sampling) are standard and easy to replicate. Evaluation does not require high-fidelity simulators; experiments can run on a modern multi-core CPU with 32 GB RAM and take a few hours of computation. The most technically demanding part is correctly implementing the shape-based equivalence class logic to compute coverage metrics.
